title: ONAN SPILLED HIS SEED, BUT WAS THAT REALLY WHY GOD KILLED HIM? THE SIN MOST PEOPLE COMPLETELY MISS
paragraphs: ONAN SPILLED HIS SEED, BUT WAS THAT REALLY WHY GOD KILLED HIM? THE SIN MOST PEOPLE COMPLETELY MISS

Genesis 38:8–10 reveals something far more disturbing than a sexual controversy. It exposes the darkness of selfishness, the exploitation of another person's vulnerability, and the kind of hidden wickedness we still struggle to recognize in ourselves.
For generations, people have argued about what Onan did with his body while overlooking what he had already decided in his heart.
And perhaps that is precisely why this passage should disturb us.
Because you may never commit the exact act Onan committed, yet still carry the same selfishness that made his actions wicked before God.
You can attend church. Quote Scripture. Raise your hands during worship. Speak beautifully about love, sacrifice, and obedience.
And still secretly arrange your life so that other people bear the consequences of your selfishness.
Onan's story is not merely about what happened in a bedroom.
It is about what happens when someone wants the privileges of a responsibility without accepting its cost.
And God saw everything.
Genesis 38 introduces us to a family already wounded by sin. Judah had three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. His eldest son, Er, married a woman named Tamar.
But Scripture tells us that Er was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord put him to death (Genesis 38:7).
Suddenly, Tamar was a widow.

In the ancient world, widowhood could mean far more than losing a husband. It could mean losing financial security, social protection, inheritance opportunities, and the hope of establishing a family.
Tamar's future had become painfully uncertain.
Judah then instructed Onan to fulfill a customary family obligation by marrying his deceased brother's widow and raising offspring for his brother.
Genesis 38:8 records:
“Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother.” — KJV
The original Hebrew contains an important expression:
וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ — veyabbem otah
Meaning: “Perform the duty of a brother-in-law toward her.”
This describes what is commonly called levirate marriage, a practice later regulated in Deuteronomy 25:5–10.
Its purpose included preserving the deceased brother's family name and providing continuity for his household.
Onan was being asked to fulfill a responsibility that extended beyond his personal desires.
But there was a problem.
Onan knew that the offspring would not be reckoned as his own in the relevant familial sense.
And he did not want that outcome.
Genesis 38:9 says:
“And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother.”
Notice how carefully Scripture reveals his motivation.
The Hebrew reads:
כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע
Ki lo lo yihyeh hazzara.
“For the offspring would not be his.”
And the final expression makes his intention even clearer:
לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו
Levilti netan-zera le'achiv.
“So as not to give offspring to his brother.”
This is not speculation about his motives.
The biblical text explicitly tells us why he acted as he did.
Onan deliberately prevented the very outcome that his responsibility toward Tamar and his deceased brother was intended to accomplish.
The Hebrew expression describing his physical action is:
וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה — veshichet artsah
The expression conveys wasting or destroying the seed upon the ground. In context, it describes an act of interrupted intercourse intended to prevent conception.
The passage also uses a construction that naturally conveys repeated behavior: whenever he went in to his brother's wife, he acted to prevent the intended offspring.
Think about what that meant for Tamar.
Onan was willing to engage in marital intimacy with her, but he deliberately frustrated the purpose of the obligation he had undertaken.
He wanted the benefit.
He refused the responsibility.
He was willing to receive something from Tamar while withholding what his duty required of him.
And then comes one of the most sobering sentences in the chapter:
“And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also.” — Genesis 38:10, KJV
The original Hebrew says:
וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה
Vayyera be'enei YHWH asher asah.
“What he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
God did not merely see the physical act.
God knew the intention Scripture had already exposed.
Now, does this passage specifically condemn masturbation?
The text does not describe masturbation. It describes intercourse deliberately interrupted to prevent conception.
Does it establish a universal prohibition against every form of contraception?

Genesis 38:8–10 alone does not explicitly establish such a universal prohibition. Christian traditions differ in their broader understanding of contraception and sexual ethics, but responsible biblical interpretation must distinguish those theological conclusions from what this particular passage directly states.
We must never force Scripture to say more than it says.
Neither should we make it say less.
Onan's physical behavior was part of his wrongdoing. But separating that behavior from his explicitly stated intention would mean ignoring the very context God preserved for us.
His sin involved deliberate disobedience, selfish refusal of familial responsibility, and conduct that exploited Tamar's vulnerable circumstances.
Inheritance and personal advantage may also have influenced his decision, although Scripture does not explicitly identify financial gain as his motive.
What Scripture does establish is that Onan did not want to provide offspring for his brother.
And that is where this ancient story begins to confront our modern hearts.
Because how many people today want the benefits of marriage without the responsibilities of marriage?
How many want loyalty without being loyal?
Forgiveness without repentance?
Leadership without accountability?
Intimacy without commitment?
The blessings of God without surrendering to God?
How many people keep someone close because of what that person provides, while having little concern for what their own selfishness is doing to that person's soul?
Perhaps you have been Tamar in someone else's story.
You trusted someone who promised to protect you.
You gave your time, your affection, your loyalty, your strength.
And slowly, painfully, you discovered that they were more interested in what they could receive from you than in how their actions affected you.
They wanted your presence but not your well-being.
Your sacrifice but not your security.
Your forgiveness but not the responsibility of changing.
And you were left wondering whether God noticed.
Genesis 38 reminds us that He does.
But before we become too comfortable identifying with Tamar, we must allow Scripture to ask us a harder question.
What if, somewhere in our own lives, we have been Onan?
What if we have accepted another person's sacrifices while refusing to make our own?
What if we have used spiritual language to disguise personal ambition?
What if our obedience has always come with an invisible condition: that we will obey God only when obedience benefits us?
We may condemn Onan because his sin seems scandalous.
Yet selfishness becomes remarkably respectable when we learn how to dress it in religious clothing.
Jesus confronted this kind of hypocrisy.
In Matthew 23:28, He warned about appearing righteous outwardly while being filled inwardly with hypocrisy and lawlessness.
And in Mark 7:21–23, Jesus explained that evil actions emerge from within the human heart.
The Greek word used for covetousness in Mark 7:22 is πλεονεξίαι — pleonexiai, conveying greed or the desire to have more.
Sin is not merely a collection of outward behaviors.
It is also a corruption of our desires, intentions, and loyalties.
That is why Christianity cannot be reduced to looking respectable.
You can modify your behavior without surrendering your heart.
You can hide your wrongdoing from everyone around you without hiding a single thing from God.
Hebrews 4:13 reminds us that all things are exposed before the eyes of the One to whom we must give account.
If this is uncovering something you have been avoiding, do not rush past that conviction.
Not to prove your righteousness to strangers.
Not because typing words can replace repentance.
But because sometimes acknowledging the truth is an important beginning in bringing our hidden struggles before Christ.
And Tamar's story was not finished when Onan died.
Judah subsequently told her to remain a widow until his youngest son, Shelah, grew up. Yet when Shelah was grown, Tamar was not given to him.
Once again, she was left waiting for a responsibility someone else had failed to fulfill.
The story eventually takes another scandalous turn involving Tamar disguising herself, Judah failing to recognize her, and Tamar becoming pregnant by him.
When Judah discovered the pregnancy, he initially demanded that she be punished.
But Tamar produced evidence revealing that Judah himself was responsible.
And suddenly, the man who had been so ready to condemn someone else was confronted with his own wrongdoing.
Genesis 38:26 records Judah's admission:
“She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son.”
The Hebrew expression is:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי — tsadqah mimmenni
“She is more righteous than I.”
This is not necessarily a declaration that every action Tamar took was morally ideal.
It is Judah's acknowledgment that, in this situation, she had a stronger claim to righteousness than he did because he had failed in his responsibility toward her.
The scandal exposed the hypocrisy.
The hidden truth became visible.
And the man who had condemned another was forced to acknowledge his own guilt.
How many families would begin healing if someone finally stopped defending their pride long enough to say, “I was wrong”?
How many marriages could begin rebuilding trust if excuses were replaced with genuine repentance?
How many churches would become healthier if accountability mattered more than protecting reputations?
Sometimes the most spiritually significant words you can speak are not the words of an impressive prayer.
Sometimes they are simply:
I sinned. I was wrong. Please forgive me.
But here is where Genesis 38 becomes something far greater than a disturbing account of human failure.
Centuries later, when Matthew recorded the genealogy of Jesus Christ, he wrote:
“And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar.” — Matthew 1:3, KJV
Judah.
Perez.
Zerah.
Tamar.
There she was.
The widow whose future had been threatened.
The woman whose circumstances were surrounded by betrayal, neglect, and scandal.
Her name appeared in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
God did not erase her from the story to make the family history look more respectable.
He preserved her name.
And through the family line of Judah and Perez came the promised Messiah.
Jesus Christ.
The inclusion of Tamar in Christ's genealogy does not mean that God approved of every sinful action committed throughout that family history.
It means human wickedness did not defeat His redemptive purposes.
God's grace is powerful enough to work through the brokenness of human history without calling evil good.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin is insignificant.
Not that consequences disappear.
Not that every earthly wound will be healed exactly as we desire.

But that Jesus Christ came into a world filled with broken people, bore our sins upon the cross, died, and rose again so that those who repent and believe in Him may receive forgiveness and eternal life.
Where Onan sought personal benefit while refusing costly responsibility, Jesus willingly gave Himself for others.
Mark 10:45 says:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
The Greek expression λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν — lytron anti pollon means “a ransom for many.”
Jesus did not come to exploit our vulnerability.
He came to redeem us.
He did not demand that we first make ourselves worthy of His love.
Romans 5:8 declares that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
He gave what we could never earn.
He paid what we could never repay.
And He calls us to a life transformed by that grace.
If you have been wounded by someone else's selfishness, Christ sees you. Forgiveness does not require you to remain in an abusive situation, excuse wrongdoing, or abandon wise boundaries.
If you have been the one causing the wounds, Christ calls you to repentance. Genuine repentance involves more than regret; it requires turning away from sin and, where possible, making things right.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia, commonly translated as repentance, conveys a change of mind that, in its biblical context, involves turning toward God.
And grace is not permission to continue exploiting the people Jesus commands us to love.
It is the undeserved mercy that teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 tells us that God's grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires.
The Gospel does not merely rescue us from the penalty of sin.
It calls us out of the patterns of sin that have been destroying our lives and the lives of others.

Not simply because it revealed something you may never have understood about Genesis 38, but because there may come a day when selfishness begins disguising itself as something reasonable in your own heart.
Return to these Scriptures when that happens.
You never know who is silently carrying a wound behind the photographs they post.
You never know who is desperately searching for a reason to believe that their painful history does not have to define their future.
Let us build a community where biblical truth is not diluted, grace is not cheapened, and broken people are continually pointed toward Jesus Christ.
You may choose to include this support as part of your regular Christian giving or voluntary offerings, according to your convictions and circumstances.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come willingly from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You cannot purchase God's favor.
You cannot buy salvation.
But if this ministry has nourished your faith, supporting its work is one meaningful way to help make that nourishment available to others.
Every act of willing generosity matters.
Before you leave, ask yourself one question.
Am I following Jesus because I genuinely love Him, or because I only want what He can give me?
Onan wanted the benefit without the responsibility.
Judah wanted to condemn another before confronting himself.
Tamar lived through the consequences of other people's failures.
Yet generations later, her name stood within the genealogy of the Savior.
What a powerful reminder that the darkest chapters of human history cannot overthrow the redemptive purposes of God.
Bring your hidden selfishness to Christ.
Bring your shame.
Bring your broken promises, your wounded heart, your failures, and the parts of your history you wish nobody knew.
Repent. Believe. Receive His mercy. Walk in obedience.
Your past may explain some of your wounds, but it does not have to become the master of your future.
Jesus Christ is greater than the scandal, greater than the shame, and greater than the sin that once held you captive.
The world may remember the chapter where everything went wrong, but the cross declares that sin does not have to write the final sentence.
